---
title: "Is the optimised geometry laterally and directionally stable?"
---

{{< include _model.qmd >}}

```{python}
ENTRY_CEILING = 90.0
SOLVE_BUDGET = 15.0
PROBE_POOL = 200.0
PROBE_SPENT = 64.3

import aerosandbox as asb
import aerosandbox.numpy as np

opt_res = get_optimised_geometry_state(get_airplane)
plane = opt_res['airplane']
v_trim = opt_res['v']
alpha_trim = opt_res['alpha']

op_beta = asb.OperatingPoint(velocity=v_trim, alpha=alpha_trim, beta=1.0)
aero_beta = asb.AeroBuildup(airplane=plane, op_point=op_beta).run()

Cl_beta = aero_beta['Cl'][0] / np.radians(1)
Cn_beta = aero_beta['Cn'][0] / np.radians(1)
```

**Answer.** It is laterally stable but directionally unstable. The dihedral effect is correct ([`{python} f"{Cl_beta:.3f} rad⁻¹"`]{.key}), but the weathercock stability is negative ([`{python} f"{Cn_beta:.3f} rad⁻¹"`]{.key}).

To minimise sink rate, the optimiser removed the nose ballast and shifted the wings far forward ([how low can trimmed sink rate be driven with free geometry and ballast?](2026-09-29-01-how-low-can-trimmed-sink-rate-be-driven-with-free-geometry-and-ballast.qmd)) to hit the 10% static margin. Because the cosmetic engine nacelles and cannons are attached to the wings, they were carried far forward of the new center of gravity (@fig-three-view), where their side area destabilises the aircraft in yaw.
